extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent lawyers, patent agents, and law students (practitioners studying obviousness doctrine)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing obviousness of patent claims in Canada (including the Windsurfing/Cripps tests, s.28.3 claim-date rules, motivation/climate, and special considerations for inventions arising from experimentation and selection patents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 28.3 (claim-date obviousness requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter defined by a claim in an application for a patent in Canada must be subject-matter that would not have been obvious on the claim date to a person skilled in the art or science to which it pertains, having regard to (a) information disclosed more than one year before the filing date by the applicant (or derived from the applicant) and (b) information disclosed before the claim date by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the claim-date (priority/earlier filing) for first-to-file system. Note that “information … available to the public” may be broader than information “generally known” in the art. Consider both applicant's own prior disclosures (with one-year bars) and third-party public disclosures before the claim date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept must be found in claims (avoid 'spirit of the invention')
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not find 'the inventive concept' or resort to vague notions such as the 'spirit of the invention' outside of the claims; the claims as construed define the monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expand the inventive concept beyond properly construed claim language; avoid resurrecting older concepts like 'pith and substance' to broaden claim scope when assessing obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windsurfing/Step 4 — Are the differences obvious steps?
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewed without hindsight, do the differences between the prior art and the inventive concept constitute steps which would have been obvious to the person skilled in the art, or do they require any degree of invention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the differences are mere procedural/physical steps one would take from prior art to invention; questions may sound like 'what steps would have been required' and risk importing a 'worth-a-try' or too-high a standard. For chemistry/pharma, many steps may be trial-and-error; that context matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation / climate of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The general state of the art includes not only knowledge and information but also attitudes, trends, prejudices and expectations; courts consider the climate in the relevant field and the existing motivation to solve a recognized problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both industry-wide motivation (literature, trends) and inventor-specific motivation. Secondary factors (commercial success, awards) may be relevant. If common general knowledge biased away from the invention, that supports non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation of the inventor vs. motivation of skilled person
rubrics_metrics.description: “Motivation” may mean why the claimed inventor made the invention, or why a hypothetical skilled person would combine elements of the prior art to arrive at it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the notional skilled person had a good reason to pursue the combination (i.e., would have had a reasonable expectation of success). Distinguish general motivation (everyone seeking solution) from unique/personal motivation (only the inventor had reason to pursue it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant date for assessing skilled person's knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Under first-to-invent the relevant date was the date of invention; under first-to-file the relevant date is the claim date (earlier of Canadian filing or valid priority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the notional skilled person's common general knowledge and prior art as of the appropriate date; art arising after that date is irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmatory or predictable experiments are not inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: If an experiment merely confirms what was already known or reproduces predictable results, there is no invention in repeating it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproducing known experimental results (predictable outcomes) is confirmatory and may amount to anticipation rather than invention. Courts cite KSR: choosing among identified, predictable solutions is not inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Following instructions or predictions of others is not inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who only carry out what they were instructed to do by others are not inventors; merely verifying another's predictions is not an invention and can amount to anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technicians executing instructions are not inventors; verifying prior predictions may destroy novelty. Distinguish mere verification from following up on others' suggestions (the latter can sometimes involve invention under 'obvious to try' analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient predictability / reasonable expectation of success => obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If the expectation of success is sufficiently predictable, and the effort involved is not great, then no patentable invention may result; U.S. law requires only a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the concepts 'sufficiently predictable' and 'reasonable expectation of success' to recognize that absolute certainty is not required for obviousness; evaluate predictability in the system (mechanical vs complex biological systems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured or unexpected chemical/physical characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: No one can have a patent merely for ascertaining the properties of a known substance, but finding unexpected physical characteristics of a known compound could be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between mere measurement of known attributes (not patentable) and discovery of unexpected properties/quantum that were not obvious from prior art — the latter can support inventiveness. Consider case law (Genentech dissent) acknowledging that existence of data may be obvious while the data's content was unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Cripps question (principal test for obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Was it obvious to a skilled person in the state of knowledge existing at the date of the patent that he could manufacture the claimed product by the disclosed methods? If 'No' the patent is valid; if 'Yes' it is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Cripps formulation as a high-level test: requires operational analysis of whether prior art leads to the claimed product. The Cripps question leaves open the meaning of 'obvious' which is further elaborated by 'directly and without difficulty' and other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Led 'directly and without difficulty' standard (Cripps elaboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an invention to be obvious it must have been made from the prior art 'directly and without difficulty' — the route to the invention must be a flagstone path, plainly perceptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts caution against over-reliance on catchphrases like 'directly and without difficulty', 'worth a try', or 'routine testing'. Still, if the route is plain and leads directly to the invention, that supports obviousness; if common general knowledge biased away from the invention, that supports non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence — the inventor’s actual path is relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the extent, nature and amount of effort required to achieve the invention: time, expense, number of trials, choices made and whether experimentation was routine or prolonged and arduous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time and effort may indicate inventive ingenuity but are not determinative — a lucky hit could be uninventive; conversely, many decisions and abundant choices may indicate inventiveness. Courts have upheld findings of invention where teams experimented intensively over months with many variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness in cases involving experimentation ('obvious to try' and research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines of authority: (a) if any research is needed, the invention is not obvious; (b) 'undue experimentation' renders a discovery non-obvious; (c) highly predictable/confirmatory experiments are obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish three outcomes: (i) where trial-and-error research (unpredictable) was required -> supports non-obviousness; (ii) where undue experimentation would have been required -> supports non-obviousness; (iii) where experiments were predictable and merely confirmatory -> supports obviousness. Use factual assessment of predictability and experimental burden.
